title: Productivity and plant species identity shape the effects of mowing on the flowering of grassland forbs
content:
Reduced mowing promotes flowering only in low- to medium-productive grasslands. Here, mowing regimes can be tailored to the phenology of local forb assemblages. Rest periods and uncut refuges can preserve late-phenological species that will not reflower after mowing, while spring cuts can enhance reflowering of spring flowers like Trifolium pratense from July onwards. Frequent mowing benefits only a few species, but from May onwards, only these species persist in high-productivity grasslands.


Abstract

Flower-rich grasslands have become increasingly rare in intensively used landscapes. Restoration of these grasslands is a key strategy to halt biodiversity loss. Many restoration schemes propose reduced mowing regimes to prevent losses of flowers, but mowing can also facilitate reflowering by alleviating light competition from dominant species. However, it remains unclear which conditions determine whether reduced mowing can promote or suppress grassland flowers. Here, we examine how the effect of reduced mowing on grassland flowers is moderated by grassland productivity. On 12 fields along a productivity gradient, we established four plots with different mowing regimes (three to zero cuts during the main growing season). In each plot and for each forb species, we measured flower cover over time in 3- to 5-day intervals. We then analysed the effects of mowing and productivity on flower richness and flower cover across the main growing season, on their recovery after mowing and on the flowering of individual forb species. Reducing the mowing frequency increased full-season flower cover at low-productivity sites, but this effect disappeared with increasing productivity. Full-season summed daily flower richness increased with both reduced mowing and lower productivity. The effects of mowing on flower cover and richness were strong and productivity-dependent in late spring, but disappeared in summer. After mowing, flower cover recovered more rapidly at lower productivity levels and higher mowing frequencies, while recovery rates of flower richness only increased with mowing frequency at lower productivity levels. Whether flowers recovered after mowing differed strongly among species. Half of all observed species recovered fully after a single spring cut, but only a few species recovered fully under more frequent mowing regimes. Synthesis and applications. Reduced mowing promotes flowering only in low- to medium-productive grasslands. Here, mowing regimes can be tailored to the phenology of local forb assemblages. Rest periods and uncut refuges can preserve late-phenological species that will not reflower after mowing, while spring cuts can enhance reflowering of spring flowers like Trifolium pratense from July onwards. Frequent mowing benefits only a few species, but from May onwards, only these species persist in high-productivity grasslands.
